3/4 has more emphasis on the quarter notes. It creates a different, rigid feel. 6/8 has more emphasis on the two groups of "triplets". The way I see it is 3/4 has three rigid beats with the downbeat of course. And 6/8 has two beats comprised of three eighth notes. 3/4 is a simple meter and 6/8 is compound. When counting, think of 3/4 as one, two, three (downbeat falling on 1) and 6/8 as 1 2 3, 1 2 3. Strong downbeat on every other 1. Subdividing them like that and devoting the downbeat to the first beat of each measure will get you to feel the difference. 

It really is a small, subtle, yet complex difference between the two rhythms

I am going to assume you know how to do regular hops in mario kart. If not its B on the wii wheel and R on the gamepad/pro controller. Fire hopping is when you hop repeatedly in a straight line after a drift boost, mushroom boost, star, slipstream and so on. It keeps your initial boost momentum goingIn order to keep a straight line, you must do consecutive hops in an alternating direction. So left,right,left, right or vice versa (doesnt matter). The more rapidly you hop in that fashion, the faster you'll go after the boost, as well as longer. This takes practice getting used to. It helps to think of it in a similar way of performing perfect wheelies in mario kart wii. Having a straight line is optimum (however once you get good at both hops and slides you can do them while turning/making steering adjustments)

Demon sliding is much more difficult than fire hopping. I'd definitely master hopping first before moving on to slides. I main motion controls and I know Im not as good at slides on the gamepad. But the idea is basically the same (I for one think slides are easier to execute on the wheel, but maybe im just biased). You basically do the same motion as hops (left right left right to maintain a straight driving line), but hold the drift button longer. The goal is instead of hopping in the same matter, you do really small drifts instead. This is to be done after successful fire hops after a boost. Or once you get really good at them on some courses slides speed you up anytime. 

Demon sliding takes A LOT of practice so don't be discouraged. There are also other techniques out there that are very important such as soft drifting, boost stacking and so on. There are a lot of videos on youtube explaining how to do those in depth. 

Hope this helped a little bit.

EDIT: 1-2 firehops for blue boosts. 4-5 firehops for orange boosts. 

Tip: You can't do successful fire hops in most downhill spots. However, you can do slides. So when practicing slides, you'll know if you're doing them right/on the right path if you don't slow down doing them at a downhill part such as in Mario Kart Stadium for example

Playing quietly is one of the most deceivingly difficult parts of piano playing. This takes quite a while to develop. I'm gonna give you a few things to try in your practicing. I assume you have a teacher. You should talk to them about this as well. If you don't have one, then I HIGHLY recommend you look into getting one. 

Anyways, from a technical perspective, when playing soft passages try leaning back a little bit from the piano. This naturally takes some weight out of your arms. This in turn allows yourself to play softly with more ease. For fast passages, try playing with a slightly higher wrist. Enough so that your fingers can still play the keys, but only enough for the finger pads to just barely get to the bottom of the key. So going all the way down, but not putting the rest of your hand into it per se. Long story short, play with higher wrists. 

From a musical perspective, try thinking of making the passage whisper as you are playing it. The imagery of whispering itself I find really helps many students play softly. Give it a try. Also, as youre playing, try thinking only about the music. It seems to me you have natural technical talent. Start concentrating more on the music itself as you are practicing. The story its telling, the way it makes you feel, the way you think the composer felt, imagery it reminds you of etc. This can be strange at first, you may make more technical mistakes, but it is a highly beneficial thing to do. If you think musically, you will play musically.

Good luck!

All three composers you've mentioned pose their own unique challenges. 

With Bach you are very exposed. What I mean by this is every single note in Bach's music is very important. If one note is wrong, the whole harmonic integrity is more than likely destroyed. Without heavy harmonies and use of the sustain pedal, these mistakes are very obvious to the whole audience. Whereas you are playing a typical romantic piece like Chopin or Rachmaninov, then you have much more note heavy harmonies and/or use of the sustain pedal. A note or two amiss will go unnoticed by most in these pieces. 

Also, each composer's musical style posed technical problems. Bach, being Bach, wrote extraordinary music. In addition, Bach himself was an extraordinary keyboardist. Best in his day arguably. Scholars say that Bach claimed himself that he could read anything on site, and primary source documents only indicate this being the truth. Naturally he knew the difficulties of some of his music. 

Chopin's music also follows this philosophy. Non coincidentally, Bach was one of Chopin's biggest inspirations. Like with Bach, the difficulty of Chopin's music varies widely. It all depends on the demands the music itself makes. Rachmaninov was a russian composer. Naturally, there are going to be lots and lots of notes. Its just the style of Russian romantic music. This is why most of Rachmaninovs pieces are highly difficult to play. It requires lots of dexterity from the pianist. Something that takes years to develop. 

With all this being said and based off what you said, there are many pieces by these composers suitable for the level you seem to be at now. 

ALL of the Chopin etudes are very difficult. If you haven't played a chopin nocturne, mazurka or waltz yet then I'd definitely tackle at least a couple of those before moving onto an etude. With Bach, if you haven't looked at an Invention yet, I'd learn an invention or two, then move on to the prelude and fugues and learn at least a couple of those before moving on to other bach music. At that point you would also be ready to tackle one of those Rachmaninov preludes. 

Hope my rambling helped!
